'''Santana''' is an American [[Rock Music|rock]] band formed in [[San Francisco]], California, in 1966 by Mexican-born American guitarist [[Carlos Santana]].<ref>{{Cite news |author=Aidin Vaziri |date=October 20, 2023 |title=Journey announces 50th anniversary tour dates — without Bay Area stops |url=https://datebook.sfchronicle.com/music/journey-freedom-tour-2024-18388109 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240424133204/https://datebook.sfchronicle.com/music/journey-freedom-tour-2024-18388109 |archive-date=April 24, 2024 |access-date=2024-05-23 |newspaper=San Francisco Chronicle |language=en-US}}</ref> The band has undergone various recording and performing line-ups in its history, with Santana being the only consistent member. After signing with [[Columbia Records]], the band's appearance at the [[Woodstock Festival]] in 1969 increased their profile and they went on to record the critically acclaimed and commercially successful albums ''[[Santana (1969 album)|Santana]]'' (1969), ''[[Abraxas (album)|Abraxas]]'' (1970) and ''[[Santana (1971 album)|Santana III]]'' (1971). These were recorded by the group's "classic" line-up, comprising organist and lead vocalist [[Gregg Rolie]], percussionists [[José Areas|José "Chepito" Areas]] and [[Michael Carabello]], drummer [[Michael Shrieve]] and bassist [[David Brown (American musician)|David Brown]]. Hit songs of this period include "[[Evil Ways (Santana song)|Evil Ways]]" (1970), "[[Black Magic Woman]]" (1970), "[[Oye Como Va]]" (1971) and the instrumental "[[Samba Pa Ti (instrumental)|Samba Pa Ti]]" (1973).

Following a change in line-up and musical direction in 1972, the band experimented with elements of [[jazz fusion]] on ''[[Caravanserai (album)|Caravanserai]]'' (1972), ''[[Welcome (Santana album)|Welcome]]'' (1973) and ''[[Borboletta]]'' (1974). The band reached a new peak of critical and commercial success with their eighteenth album, ''[[Supernatural (Santana album)|Supernatural]]'' (1999), which included the [[Billboard Hot 100|''Billboard'' Hot 100]]-number one singles "[[Smooth (Santana song)|Smooth]]" (featuring [[Rob Thomas (musician)|Rob Thomas]]) and "[[Maria Maria]]" (featuring [[The Product G&B]]). The album peaked atop the charts in eleven countries and sold 12&nbsp;million copies domestically. It won eight [[Grammy Awards]] at the [[42nd Annual Grammy Awards]], a record tied with [[Michael Jackson]] and three [[Latin Grammy Awards]].<ref>{{cite web |title= Adele To Michael Jackson: Who's Won The Most GRAMMYs In A Night? |date= 15 May 2017 |publisher= [[The Recording Academy]]. |url= https://www.grammy.com/grammys/news/adele-michael-jackson-whos-won-most-grammys-night |access-date= February 8, 2019 |archive-date= 10 March 2019 |archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20190310003104/https://www.grammy.com/grammys/news/adele-michael-jackson-whos-won-most-grammys-night |url-status= live }}</ref> In 2014, the "classic" line-up—with the exception of Brown, who died in 2000—reunited for ''[[Santana IV]]'' (2016) and the group continue to perform and record.

Santana is one of the [[List of best-selling music artists|best-selling groups of all time]], with over 47&nbsp;million certified records sold in the US and an estimated 100&nbsp;million sold worldwide.<ref name="RIAAsales">{{cite web|url=https://www.riaa.com/gold-platinum/?tab_active=top_tallies&ttt=TAA#search_section|title=Gold & Platinum – Top Tallies – Top Artists (Albums)|publisher=Recording Industry Association of America|access-date=May 18, 2019|archive-date=3 December 2017|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20171203033345/https://www.riaa.com/gold-platinum/?tab_active=top_tallies&ttt=TAA#search_section|url-status=live}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.jacksonville.com/entertainment/music/2017-10-19/echoes-woodstock-santana-one-few-big-names-still-road|title=Echoes of Woodstock: Santana one of the few big names still on the road|work=[[The Florida Times-Union]]|first=Tom|last=Szaroleta|date=October 19, 2017|access-date=October 19, 2017|archive-date=19 October 2017|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20171019231609/http://www.jacksonville.com/entertainment/music/2017-10-19/echoes-woodstock-santana-one-few-big-names-still-road|url-status=live}}</ref> Its [[Santana discography|discography]] includes 25 studio albums, 14 of which reached the US Top 10. In 1998, the line-up of Santana, Rolie, Carabello, Shrieve, Brown and Areas was inducted into the [[Rock and Roll Hall of Fame]].<ref name=RRHOF>[https://www.rockhall.com/inductees/santana "Santana"] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160826235738/https://www.rockhall.com/inductees/santana |date=26 August 2016 }}. Rock and Roll Hall of Fame. Retrieved 15 February 2024.</ref>

==History==
===1966–1972: Formation and breakthrough===
In 1966, Mexican-born American musician [[Carlos Santana]] discovered San Francisco's [[hippie]] and [[counterculture]] movement and found himself "wanting to be part of this new wave."<ref name=RS72>{{cite web|url=https://www.rollingstone.com/music/music-news/the-resurrection-of-santana-228986/|title=The Resurrection of Santana|first=Ben|last=Fong-Torres|date=December 7, 1972|publisher=Rolling Stone|access-date=August 26, 2022}}</ref> Later that year, he began to assemble his own band, the first line-up of which included Sergio "Gus" Rodriguez on bass, Danny Haro on drums, and [[Michael Carabello]] on percussion. In January 1967, the four were granted an audition spot for concert promoter [[Bill Graham (promoter)|Bill Graham]] at the [[The Fillmore|Fillmore Auditorium]] on a bill with the [[Paul Butterfield]] Blues Band and the [[Charles Lloyd (jazz musician)|Charles Lloyd Quartet]], and named themselves the Santana Blues Band.<ref>{{citation |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=60Jde3l7WNwC&pg=PA137 | title=Legends of rock guitar |first1=Pete |last1=Prown |first2=Harvey P. |last2=Newquist |first3=Jon F. |last3=Eiche |access-date=2015-08-24| isbn=978-0-7935-4042-6 | year=1997 | publisher=Hal Leonard Corporation }}</ref> Within a month, the group expanded with the addition of Tom Fraser on guitar and vocals, who also brought in [[Gregg Rolie]] on organ and vocals.<ref name=RS72/> The band stalled for several weeks, however, after Carlos was hospitalised with [[tuberculosis]]. In June 1967, Graham fired the group from performing at the Fillmore after some members turned up late for a gig supporting [[The Who]] and [[Loading Zone]]. The incident drove Carlos to bring in new and committed musicians, keeping Rolie with him.<ref name=RS72/> By the year's end, the band adopted the shorter name of Santana. Until early 1969, the band were joined by [[Marcus Malone]] on percussion, who left the group after being convicted of manslaughter.<ref name=RS72/>

In late 1968, the group secured a record deal with [[Columbia Records]], following a successful audition opening for the [[Grateful Dead]]. The band had caught the interest of Columbia and [[Atlantic Records]], and an audition was organised for both labels, but Carlos refused to perform for Atlantic as he wanted to be on the same label as [[Miles Davis]] and [[Bob Dylan]].{{sfn|Leng|2000|p=40}} In December, Santana performed a series of concerts at the Fillmore that were recorded for a proposed live album. Biographer Simon Leng said it marked Santana moving away from its blues and R&B roots towards the "Santana sound" with the addition of Afro-Cuban and jazz numbers into their sets.{{sfn|Leng|2000|p=42}} After several line-up changes, the group finally stabilised in May 1969 with Santana, Rolie, Carabello, [[David Brown (American musician)|David Brown]] on bass, [[Michael Shrieve]] on drums, and [[Jose Areas|Jose "Chepito" Areas]] on percussion, which became known as the "classic" line-up.<ref name="TGG83">{{cite web|url=https://www.rocksbackpages.com/Library/Article/carlos-santana-2|title=The Guitar Greats – Carlos Santana|first1=Stuart|last1=Grundy|first2=John|last2=Tobler|publisher=BBC Books|year=1983|via=[[Rock's Backpages]]|url-access=subscription}}</ref>

[[File:Woodstock redmond stage.JPG|thumb|right|Santana rose to prominence following their appearance at Woodstock]]
The band recorded their debut album, ''[[Santana (1969 album)|Santana]]'', in San Francisco in May 1969. It was their third go at recording an album, after previous attempts failed to produce results they wanted. The sessions featured Alberto Gianquinto on piano, who also helped with the arrangements of the tracks. He quickly noticed the group's main problem: the solo spots were too long.{{sfn|Leng|2000|p=46}} Graham agreed, and advised that the band needed to cut the lengthy jams and begin constructing songs. He also got the band to listen to [[Willie Bobo]]'s version of "[[Evil Ways (Santana song)|Evil Ways]]", and suggested they record their own version.{{sfn|Leng|2000|p=46}} With the album recorded, Graham arranged for Santana to tour the Midwest as openers for [[Crosby, Stills and Nash]], which expanded the group's profile outside the West Coast.{{sfn|Leng|2000|p=48}} Around this time, Graham had been asked to help organise the upcoming [[Woodstock Festival]] and agreed to promote it on the condition that Santana would be added to the bill. Graham persisted, and the band were assigned a 45-minute set in the afternoon of August 16, the second day, for $2,500.{{sfn|Leng|2000|p=49}} The performance launched the group to international fame, and ''Santana'', released on August 30, peaked at No. 4 on the US [[Billboard 200|''Billboard'' 200]]. The first single, "[[Jin-go-lo-ba|Jingo]]", was followed by "Evil Ways", which peaked at No. 9 on the ''Billboard'' [[Billboard Hot 100|Hot 100]]. In October 1969, Graham had Santana perform at the [[Gold Rush (music festival)|Gold Rush]] rock music festival and on ''[[The Ed Sullivan Show]]'', further increasing the group's nationwide exposure.{{sfn|Leng|2000|p=48}}<ref>{{Cite web |last=Lynn |first=Canning |date=April 29, 2019 |title=1969 Amador Gold Rush Music Festival |url=https://www.eaglemagazine.com/departments/close-up/my-life-in-rock-and-roll/ |access-date=2023-09-15 |website=Eagle Magazine |language=en-US |archive-date=22 September 2023 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230922235425/https://www.eaglemagazine.com/departments/close-up/my-life-in-rock-and-roll/ |url-status=live }}</ref>

In April 1970, Santana returned to the studio to record its second album, ''[[Abraxas (album)|Abraxas]]''.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=eikEAAAAMBAJ&q=pacific+high+recording+studioas&pg=PA55 |title=Billboard |date=1970-06-27 |access-date=2015-08-24}}</ref> The album, highlighted by a reworking of "[[Black Magic Woman]]" by [[Fleetwood Mac]] that peaked at No. 4 in the US [[Billboard Hot 100|''Billboard'' Hot 100]], was released in September 1970 and rose to number 1 on the US [[Billboard 200|''Billboard'' 200]].

By 1971, the group were still struggling to maintain a strong musical direction.<ref name="TGG83" /> From January to July they recorded ''[[Santana (1971 album)|Santana III]]''. Released in September 1971, the album also reached number 1 on the US ''Billboard'' 200. At the peak of the band's popularity, the album was the last to feature its classic Woodstock era line-up. Santana explained that there was a lot of unnecessary internal resentment and that managerial problems contributed to the problem, leading to Graham's dismissal.<ref name="TGG83" /> That year, they performed at a concert in [[Accra]] to commemorate [[Ghana]]'s 14th [[Independence Day (Ghana)|Independence Day]]. The concert was filmed and released in theaters as ''[[Soul to Soul (film)|Soul to Soul]]''.<ref>{{Cite news|url=https://www.nytimes.com/1971/08/19/archives/rousing-soul-to-soul.html|title=Rousing 'Soul to Soul'|last=Thompson|first=Howard|date=August 19, 1971|work=The New York Times|access-date=22 September 2019|archive-date=24 March 2022|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220324183205/https://www.nytimes.com/1971/08/19/archives/rousing-soul-to-soul.html|url-status=live}}</ref> Matters came to a head shortly before the ''Santana III'' tour in September 1971 began, when Carlos wanted Carabello to leave the group, otherwise Carlos himself would quit. The band started the tour without Carlos, performing amidst shouts from the audience for the guitarist. After several gigs, Carlos reunited with the band to find Carabello, Areas, and manager/promoter Stan Marcum had quit, leaving the band to perform without percussionists. [[Mingo Lewis|James "Mingo" Lewis]] was quickly brought in as a temporary replacement after he saw the band live and offered his services.{{sfn|Leng|2000|pp=64–65}} Santana's gig in [[Lima]], Peru in December 1971 brought further trouble, as the outbreak of violence resulted in their equipment being confiscated and the band deported from the country. The incident was a wake-up call for Carlos, who was determined to "bring the madness to an end."{{sfn|Leng|2000|pp=64–65}}

In 1972, Santana had been increasingly influenced by the music of [[Miles Davis]], [[John Coltrane]], and [[Joe Zawinul]], who had explored jazz fusion by this time.<ref name="TGG83" /> The fourth album, ''[[Caravanserai (album)|Caravanserai]]'' (1972), marked a number of line-up changes; bassist David Brown left in 1971 before recording started and was replaced by Doug Rauch and Tom Rutley. Carabello was replaced with two percussionists, Armando Peraza and Mingo Lewis. Rolie was replaced by [[Tom Coster]] on a few songs. ''Caravanserai'' debuted at number 8 in the US.

===1973–1979: Experimentation and consolidation===
[[File:Santana 1973 (cropped).jpg|thumb|upright|Carlos Santana in 1973]]
13 months after ''Caravanserai'', Santana released ''[[Welcome (Santana album)|Welcome]]''. ''Welcome'' was the first of four consecutive albums to achieve gold certification, as opposed to the previous four, which all at least reached platinum status. The album peaked at number 25 on the ''Billboard'' 200, the lowest of the band's career so far. The next few albums contained a more experimental style than their previous work, beginning with ''[[Borboletta]]'', which fared arguably worse than its predecessor, despite climbing five spots higher on the Billboard album charts in the US.

The group's 1976 release, ''[[Amigos (Santana album)|Amigos]]'', was far more successful. Reaching number 10 on the US charts, and also hitting the top 10 in France, Australia, New Zealand, Austria and the Netherlands, it was a return to the success of their early albums. ''[[Festival (Santana album)|Festival]]'', did not obtain the same newfound success, but was followed by another successful album, ''[[Moonflower (album)|Moonflower]]'', released in 1977. The album was possibly the most successful since ''Santana III'', achieving 2× platinum in the US, and being the first album since 1974's ''Borboletta'', to break the top 10 in the UK. It was characterized by a stylistic shift for the band, as it contained heavier influences from the more conventional sound of the group's early work, while still maintaining the experimental sound of their last few albums.

Their next two releases, ''[[Inner Secrets]]'' and ''[[Marathon (Santana album)|Marathon]]'', released in 1978 and '79, respectively, were a further musical shift for the band, moving away from the Latin-fused rock music that had characterized their work in the late 1960s and the majority of the '70s, to move towards a more album-oriented, conventional rock sound. These albums, however, fared poorly commercially, although both achieved gold status in the US.

===1980–1997: Commercial decline and seven-year hiatus===
The 1980s started relatively brightly for Santana, with 1981's platinum-selling ''[[Zebop!]]'', which also reached the top 20 in several countries, and continued the more conventional rock sound. The following year, ''[[Shangó (Santana album)|Shangó]]'' was released; this album marked a steep decline in the band's commercial fortunes, although it still achieved gold status.

The group waited another three years to release the follow-up, the longest break for them so far. 1985's ''[[Beyond Appearances]]'' was a commercial failure, and their first album not to achieve gold certification. Their following three releases all continued this commercial decline, with the last of these failing to break the ''Billboard'' top 100. In the midst of this commercial pitfall, the band stopped recording material for an unprecedented seven years but continued to tour.

===1998–2001: ''Supernatural'' and the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame===
In 1998, Santana was inducted into the [[Rock and Roll Hall of Fame]]. The following year, their album ''[[Supernatural (Santana album)|Supernatural]]'' (1999) debuted at number 19 on the ''Billboard'' 200 and reached No. 1 after eighteen weeks. Also reaching No. 1 were two singles: "[[Smooth (Santana song)|Smooth]]", recorded with [[Rob Thomas (musician)|Rob Thomas]], and "[[Maria Maria]]" featuring [[The Product G&B]]. The album was certified platinum 15 times by the [[RIAA]] and sold 30&nbsp;million copies worldwide.<ref>{{cite web |title=Gold & Platinum Turns 60! |url=https://www.riaa.com/goldandplatinum60/#cd-era |website=RIAA |access-date=7 June 2024 |date=2018 |archive-date=26 April 2018 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180426080241/https://www.riaa.com/goldandplatinum60/#cd-era |url-status=live }}</ref><ref>{{cite web |last1=DHNS |title=Viva Santana! |url=https://www.deccanherald.com/content/292577/viva-santana.html |website=Deccan Herald |access-date=7 June 2024 |language=en |date=17 November 2012 |archive-date=2 November 2013 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20131102002220/http://www.deccanherald.com/content/292577/viva-santana.html |url-status=live }}</ref> Santana's previous number one album had been ''[[Santana (1971 album)|Santana III]]'' in 1971. According to ''[[Guinness World Records]]'', this is the longest gap between number one albums.<ref>{{Cite web |date=October 1999 |title=Longest gap between US chart album hits |url=https://www.guinnessworldrecords.com/world-records/76351-longest-gap-between-us-chart-album-hits |access-date=July 1, 2024 |website=Guinness World Records}}</ref><ref>Although other gaps between albums that top the charts may be longer, no one else has applied for this record, leaving this still as the official record</ref>

''Supernatural'' won eight Grammy Awards, including the award for [[Grammy Award for Album of the Year|Album of the Year]],<ref>{{cite web |title=42nd Annual GRAMMY Awards |url=https://www.grammy.com/awards/42nd-annual-grammy-awards |website=grammy.com |access-date=7 June 2024 |archive-date=8 March 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220308120651/https://www.grammy.com/awards/42nd-annual-grammy-awards |url-status=live }}</ref> and also won three [[Latin Grammy Awards]].<ref>{{cite magazine |last1=Grow |first1=Kory |title='I Felt Really, Really High': Carlos Santana Looks Back on His Historic 2000 Grammy Night |url=https://www.rollingstone.com/music/music-features/carlos-santana-grammys-2000-supernatural-smooth-interview-953333/ |magazine=Rolling Stone |access-date=7 June 2024 |date=21 February 2020}}</ref>

===2002–2012: Dealing with newfound success===
[[File:Santana Acer Arena (5558204467).jpg|thumb|upright=1.25|Santana performing in 2011]]
The follow-up to ''Supernatural'' came three years later and was highly anticipated by international media and fans alike. On October 22, 2002, ''[[Shaman (album)|Shaman]]'' was released worldwide. Although it initially sold briskly (298,973 copies in the US in its first week) and debuted at number 1 on the ''Billboard'' 200, the album's appeal quickly wore off and it soon slid down the charts. Despite this, it went on to sell 2× platinum in the US, and achieved platinum status in several other countries including Australia. The first single released from the album, "[[The Game of Love (Santana song)|The Game of Love]]", which featured vocals from [[Michelle Branch]], debuted at number 5 on the Hot 100. The album's next four singles failed to chart in most countries, but the final single, "[[Why Don't You & I]]", featuring the vocals of [[Alex Band]], reached number 8 on the Hot 100. Musically, the album was a return to a more conventional sound for the group, with a mainly Latin rock-based sound.

With their renewed appeal worn off, another three-year wait saw the release of 2005's ''[[All That I Am (Santana album)|All That I Am]]''. The album debuted at number 2 on the ''Billboard'' 200 but fared worse internationally, and quickly lost appeal. The album, a continuation of the Latin-rock influenced sound of ''Shaman'', achieved gold certification in the US. A five-year break from recording saw the release of another studio album, ''[[Guitar Heaven]]'' (2010). Musically it was a drastic change for the band, with a far heavier sound at its core and strong [[Heavy metal music|heavy metal]] influences. It debuted at number 5 on the ''Billboard'' 200 but marked another decline for the band, failing to achieve gold status.

In 2012 the group released ''[[Shape Shifter (album)|Shape Shifter]]'', which returned to the conventional Latin rock sound and was completely album-oriented, as no singles were released from it. It debuted at number 16 on the [[Billboard 200]].

===2013–2020: Reunion of the classic line-up, ''Corazón'', ''Santana IV'', and ''Africa Speaks''===
In February 2013, Carlos Santana confirmed that he would reunite his classic line-up, most of whom played Woodstock with him in 1969. Santana stated that he was reuniting the group with the intention of recording new music. Confirmed for the reunion were Neal Schon, who was in the band in the early 1970s where he traded lead guitar work with Santana before leaving with founding Santana singer-organist Gregg Rolie in 1973 to form [[Journey (band)|Journey]]; drummer Mike Shrieve and percussionist Mike Carabello. Santana said of Rolie, who played with Ringo Starr's All-Starr Band for the last two years, "I'm pretty sure Gregg's going to do it." In February 2013, Rolie told Radio.com, "it's (the reunion) just a matter of putting it together and going and doing it. I would do it. I think it's a great idea. People would love it. It could be great!"<ref>{{cite news|access-date=20 March 2013|url=http://www.presstelegram.com/lifestyle/ci_22679861/|archive-url=https://archive.today/20130411172707/http://www.presstelegram.com/lifestyle/ci_22679861/|archive-date=11 April 2013|title= Santana Reuniting classic 60's and 70's lineup|work=Press Telegram|date=19 February 2013|author=Smith, Steve}}</ref>

Before the reunion album was released, on May 6, 2014, the then-current lineup of Santana released a new studio album entitled ''[[Corazón (Santana album)|Corazón]]''.  On September 9, 2014, this was followed by the release of ''Corazón – Live from Mexico: Live It to Believe It'', a live album (on CD, DVD and Blu-ray) of their December 14, 2013 concert in Guadalajara, Mexico.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://santana.hifi247.com/santana-corazon-live-from-mexico-live-it-to-believe-it-dvd.html |title=Santana – Corazon – Live From Mexico: Live It To Believe It DVD |date=2014 |website=Santana.hifi247.com |access-date=25 October 2014 |archive-date=25 October 2014 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20141025140537/http://santana.hifi247.com/santana-corazon-live-from-mexico-live-it-to-believe-it-dvd.html }}</ref>

On April 15, 2016, Santana released ''[[Santana IV]]'', the wildly anticipated studio album that reunited the late 1960s and early 1970s classic lineup of Carlos Santana (guitar, vocals), Gregg Rolie (keyboards, lead vocals), Neal Schon (guitar, vocals), Michael Carabello (percussion) and Michael Shrieve (drums). The album marked the first time in 45 years – since 1971's multi-platinum classic ''[[Santana (1971 album)|Santana III]]'' – that the quintet had recorded together.<ref name="facebook.com carlossantana post 25 January 2016">{{cite web |url=https://www.facebook.com/carlossantana/photos/a.94203671358.88480.9411551358/10153466174096359/?type=1&theater |title=From Team Santana: April 15th, 2016 marks the release date of Santana IV... |date= 25 January 2016 |website=[[Facebook]] |access-date= 10 February 2016}}</ref> The first single from ''Santana IV'', entitled "Anywhere You Want to Go", had been previously released on February 5, 2016.<ref name="news.iheart.com Anywhere You Want To Go">{{cite web |url=http://news.iheart.com/articles/rock-news-104703/listen-to-santana-anywhere-you-want-14327897/ |title=Listen to Santana – 'Anywhere You Want To Go' |date=1 February 2016 |website=news.iheart.com |access-date=10 February 2016 |archive-date=24 February 2016 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160224041901/http://news.iheart.com/articles/rock-news-104703/listen-to-santana-anywhere-you-want-14327897/ |url-status=live }}</ref>

The origins of the reunion went back several years, when Schon suggested that he and Carlos Santana record together. Santana liked the idea but proposed that they recruit Rolie, Shrieve and Carabello for what would be called "Santana IV". After initial writing sessions and rehearsals took place in 2013, the group recorded throughout 2014 and 2015, amassing 16 new tracks that combined all their signature elements – Afro-Latin rhythms, soaring vocals, electrifying blues-psychedelic guitar solos, and irrepressible jubilant percussion work.

About the "Santana IV" team, Santana stated: "It was magical, we didn't have to try to force the vibe – it was immense. From there, we then needed to come up with a balance of songs and jams that people would immediately identify as Santana."<ref name="santana.hifi247.com Santana IV">{{cite web |url=http://santana.hifi247.com/santana-iv-cd.html |title=Santana IV CD |date=2016 |website=santana.com |access-date=10 February 2016 |archive-date=13 February 2016 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160213005237/http://santana.hifi247.com/santana-iv-cd.html }}</ref> ''Santana IV'' features 16 all-new tracks written and produced by the band. Joining the core "Santana IV" band in the studio are current Santana members Karl Perazzo (percussion) and Benny Rietveld (bass), with vocalist [[Ronald Isley]] guesting on two cuts. 

On October 21, 2016, Santana released ''Santana IV: Live at the House of Blues Las Vegas'' on Eagle Rock Entertainment, a live album (on DVD/Blu-ray/2CD) of their concert on March 21, 2016 at [[House of Blues]] in [[Mandalay Bay Resort and Casino]] on the [[Las Vegas Strip]] in [[Nevada]].

In early January 2019, Santana signed with [[Concord Records]];<ref name="concord.com Carlos Santana signs with Concord Records">{{cite web |url=https://concord.com/concord-music-news/legendary-musician-carlos-santana-signs-with-concord-records |title=Legendary Musician Carlos Santana Signs with Concord Records |date=April 2019 |website=[[Concord Music]] |access-date=9 April 2019 |archive-date=20 April 2019 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190420183558/https://concord.com/concord-music-news/legendary-musician-carlos-santana-signs-with-concord-records/ |url-status=live }}</ref> in late January, they released ''[[In Search of Mona Lisa]]'', a new five-track EP.<ref name="AllMusic">{{cite web |url= https://www.allmusic.com/album/in-search-of-mona-lisa-mw0003237271 |title=Santana – ''In Search of Mona Lisa'': Review |first=Stephen |last=Erlewine |publisher=AllMusic |access-date=9 April 2019}}</ref> The day before, they also released a video for new single, "Do You Remember Me."<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.guitarworld.com/news/santana-premiere-do-you-remember-me-music-video|title=Santana Premiere "Do You Remember Me" Music Video|last=Maxwell|first=Jackson|website=guitarworld|date=24 January 2019|language=en|access-date=2019-01-25|archive-date=26 January 2019|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190126220819/https://www.guitarworld.com/news/santana-premiere-do-you-remember-me-music-video|url-status=live}}</ref> In March 2019, the band announced plans to release on ''[[Africa Speaks (Santana album)|Africa Speaks]]'', their new full-length album produced by [[Rick Rubin]], on June 7.<ref>{{Cite magazine|url=https://www.rollingstone.com/music/music-news/santana-rick-rubin-song-los-invisibles-809641/|title=Hear Santana's Fiery New Rick Rubin-Produced Song 'Los Invisibles'|last=Kreps|first=Daniel|date=2019-03-18|magazine=Rolling Stone|language=en-US|access-date=2019-04-09|archive-date=21 March 2019|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190321015138/https://www.rollingstone.com/music/music-news/santana-rick-rubin-song-los-invisibles-809641/|url-status=live}}</ref>

2019 marked the 20th anniversary of Carlos Santana's album ''Supernatural'' and the 50th anniversary of his performance at Woodstock. Santana headlined a multi-year residency at House of Blues. The band was expected to headline at both [[Woodstock 50]] (which was cancelled)<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.woodstock.com/|title=Woodstock 50 • Aug. 16, 17 & 18 2019 {{!}} Watkins Glen, NY|website=Woodstock 50|language=en-US|access-date=2019-04-09|archive-date=6 April 2019|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190406191503/https://www.woodstock.com/|url-status=live}}</ref> and Bethel Woods' half-centennial celebration in Bethel, NY, in August 2019.<ref>{{Cite magazine|url=https://www.rollingstone.com/music/music-news/ringo-starr-santana-bethel-woods-woodstock-796958/|title=Ringo Starr, Santana Lead Bethel Woods' 50th Anniversary of Woodstock Celebration|last=Kreps|first=Daniel|date=2019-02-20|magazine=Rolling Stone|language=en-US|access-date=2019-04-09|archive-date=6 April 2019|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190406233354/https://www.rollingstone.com/music/music-news/ringo-starr-santana-bethel-woods-woodstock-796958/|url-status=live}}</ref> The band toured in support of the latest album, from April to November 2019.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://tour.santana.com/|title=Santana Fan Club Tickets|website=tour.santana.com|language=en|access-date=2019-04-09|archive-date=6 April 2019|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190406233354/https://tour.santana.com/|url-status=live}}</ref>

===2021–2024: ''Blessings and Miracles''===
On 18 and 20 August 2021, "Move" and "She's Fire", the first and second singles taken from Santana's (then) forthcoming new album ''[[Blessings and Miracles]]'', were released; it was announced that the album would be released on 15 October 2021 via [[BMG Rights Management|BMG Entertainment]].

===2025–present: ''Sentient''===
On 21 February 2025, it was announced the upcoming release (via [[Candid Records]]) of ''Sentient'', Santana's new studio album, a retrospective of 11 tracks featuring collaborations with other artists such as [[Michael Jackson]], [[Smokey Robinson]], [[Miles Davis]], [[Paolo Rustichelli]], [[Darryl "DMC" McDaniels]] and [[Cindy Blackman Santana]],<ref name="santana.com Sentient">{{cite web |url=https://santana.com/news/santana-sentient-available-march-28 |title=Santana Sentient Available March 28! |date=2025-02-21 |publisher=Santana.com |access-date=2025-03-09}}</ref> including "Whatever Happens" (a track from Michael Jackson's last album, ''[[Invincible (Michael Jackson album)|Invincible]]''), remastered tracks such as "Let the Guitar Play" (a re-work of "Song for Cindy" from ''Blessings and Miracles'' featuring Darryl "DMC" McDaniels) or Grammy Awards winner "Blues for Salvador"... and 3 new tracks: Smokey Robinson's "Please Don't Take Your Love", "Coherence" (a track featuring Cindy Blackman Santana) and an instrumental live version of Michael Jackson's "[[Stranger in Moscow]]" recorded in 2012 with Carlos as guest of [[Narada Michael Walden]]'s band.<ref name="news.theurbanmusicscene.com Sentient">{{cite web |url=https://news.theurbanmusicscene.com/2025/02/santana-to-release-new-album-sentient |title=Guitar legend Santana to release new album "Sentient" on March 28th, 2025... |date=2025-02-21 |publisher=TheUrbanMusicScene.com |website=news.theurbanmusicscene.com |access-date=2025-03-09}}</ref> The album was released on 28 March 2025.<ref name=sentient>{{cite web |url=https://santana.com/news/santana-releases-sentient-his-passion-filled-retrospective-album |title=Santana Releases Sentient, His Passion-Filled Retrospective Album |publisher=Santana.com |date=2025-03-28 |access-date=2025-04-08}}</ref>

On 16 April 2025 in [[Highland, CA]] (at the Yaamava’ Resort & Casino at San Manuel), Santana embarked on the (8-date) Oneness North American tour which ended on 29 April 2025 in [[Nashville, TN]] (at The Pinnacle).<ref name="Oneness Tour 2025 US & Europe">[https://www.santana.com/news/santana-announces-oneness-tour-2025-us-europe-dates/ www.santana.com > news > post "Santana Announces Oneness Tour 2025 US & Europe Dates" (10 December 2024)]</ref>

On 9 June 2025 in [[Łódź]], [[Poland]] (at the [[Atlas Arena]]), Santana embarked on the (29-date) Oneness Europe and UK tour (including a show on 21 June 2025 in [[London]], [[UK]] at [[The O2]] and a 7-date leg in [[Spain]] from 26 July to 4 August 2025) due to end on 11 August 2025 in [[Copenhagen]], [[Denmark]] (at the Royal Arena).<ref name="Oneness Tour 2025 US & Europe"/>

==Awards and nominations==
{{Main|List of awards and nominations received by Santana}}

Santana has won numerous awards, including eight [[Grammy Awards]] and three [[Latin Grammy Awards]].<ref>{{cite web |title=Artist: Carlos Santana |url=https://www.grammy.com/grammys/artists/carlos-santana |publisher=[[The Recording Academy]] |date=20 November 2019 |access-date=6 December 2019 |archive-date=31 May 2020 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200531100240/https://www.grammy.com/grammys/artists/carlos-santana |url-status=live }}</ref> The band was inducted into the [[List of Rock and Roll Hall of Fame inductees|Rock and Roll Hall of Fame]] in 1998; three of Santana's albums have been inducted the [[Grammy Hall of Fame]] (''[[Abraxas (album)|Abraxas]]'' in 1999, the original ''[[Santana (1969 album)|Santana]]'' in 2012, and ''[[Supernatural (Santana album)|Supernatural]]'' in 2025); and one song has been inducted into the [[Latin Grammy Hall of Fame]] ("[[Oye Como Va]]" in 2001).
